Anarchism is the political tradition that says: nobody should rule anyone else, and we can still run complex societies — through voluntary cooperation. The word comes from Greek an-arkhia = “without a ruler”, not “without order”. WHAT ANARCHISM IS A design method: replace command hierarchies with horizontal networks. An economy: commons + cooperatives + mutual aid instead of boss-owned firms or state-owned monopolies. A peace strategy: no armies of conquest, no police as rulers — community safety, mediation, restorative justice. WHAT IT IS NOT Not “everyone does whatever they want”. Freedom stops where domination starts. Not chaos: Spanish collectives ran trains, hospitals and farms in 1936–39 with elected, recallable delegates. Not pacifism-at-all-costs for all currents: most anarchists defend self-defence but oppose war, conscription and invasion. PROMOTIONAL NOTE — WHY TRY IT? Because hierarchy wastes talent. In a cooperative, the person who does the job designs the job. Studies of worker cooperatives (Mondragón in Spain, Emilia-Romagna in Italy) show higher survival rates and pay equity. Learn them once, you can read every later chapter. 1. Mutual aid (Kropotkin) Peter Kropotkin, observing Siberian animals and peasant communes, argued cooperation — not cut-throat competition — drives evolution ( Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution , 1902). Technical form: pooled funds, tool libraries, community kitchens, strike support. Everyone contributes what they can, draws what they need in crisis. 2. Free association & voluntary federation Individuals → affinity groups → neighbourhood assemblies → federations of assemblies. Higher levels cannot command lower ones; they coordinate. Delegates carry a written mandate and can be recalled instantly. This is the opposite of a party that disciplines its base. 3. Direct action Solve the problem yourself instead of petitioning rulers: occupy empty housing to house people, create a free clinic, run a strike without union bosses. Direct action is not necessarily violent — most of it is constructive (build the alternative) and obstructive (block the harm). 4. Prefiguration Build the future in the present. If you want a non-sexist, non-racist society, your assembly must be non-sexist and non-racist now: rotation of speaking, childcare at meetings, translation, veto against oppression. 5. Solutions: cooperatives, community land trusts, open-source licenses. 6. Anti-domination (intersectional) Class, state, patriarchy, racism, colonialism, ecocide are linked hierarchies. SDK levels are not version numbers Three integers look similar and mean completely different things. Getting them confused produces apps that either crash on old phones or get rejected by Play. minSdk — the oldest Android version that may install the app. Set by device reach and library requirements. A low value costs testing surface; a high value costs users. compileSdk — the platform JAR your code compiles against. Newer APIs need a newer value. It does not change runtime behavior. targetSdk — the behavior contract at runtime. It decides whether Android applies new restrictions (background limits, notification permission, photo picker behavior). Raising it is a migration, not a checkbox. A real project shape for 2026: minSdk 26 (covers devices that still receive security updates and meets most modern library floors), compileSdk 37 , targetSdk 36 while you test 37's behavior changes. Your Compose version gates the maximum compileSdk , so upgrade Compose and AGP before jumping the SDK. It is to move the project forward one axis at a time: Gradle wrapper first, then AGP, then Kotlin and the Compose compiler, then compileSdk , then targetSdk . Bump all five at once and you will not know which one broke the build. You trade working Docker, WSL2 and device security for an emulator that is still slow — and you often break corporate security policy in the process. The Android Emulator on Windows expects WHPX; fighting it with a second hypervisor usually ends in HAXM is not installed or emulator: ERROR: x86 emulation currently requires hardware acceleration . Old HAXM instructions are obsolete on modern Windows and on Apple silicon entirely. Running two hypervisors simultaneously can fail silently, producing an emulator that boots at 3 fps. Do this instead: enable WHPX and firmware virtualization, keep Hyper-V/WSL2 as they are, and use an arm64 image on Apple silicon. If the host truly cannot accelerate, test on a physical device over USB — it is faster than a software-emulated system image. Bad decision · 03 Installing Studio with sudo , or inside a cloud-synced folder Running the Linux launcher as root leaves ~/.android , ~/.gradle and IDE config owned by root, which breaks plugins, SDK updates and file permissions later. Installing the SDK under OneDrive/Dropbox/iCloud causes file-locking and sync churn that manifests as random Gradle failures and corrupted caches. Do this instead: install per-user or to /opt with user ownership, keep the SDK outside sync folders, and set ANDROID_HOME once in your shell profile so the IDE and terminal agree. This level covers IDE settings, build memory, the Gradle Wrapper, and the three files that must never enter Git. The first-run checklist Open Settings (Windows/Linux) or Preferences (macOS) and make these decisions once, deliberately. Nothing here is cosmetic. Setting Choose Why Gradle JDK Build, Execution, Deployment → Build Tools → Gradle JDK 17 (embedded or a managed JDK) AGP 9.4 requires 17. Pointing at a random JDK 21 or 11 is a top-three build failure. IDE memory Help → Change Memory Settings 2–4 GB heap ( -Xmx4g ) on 16 GB machines Too low causes indexing stalls; too high starves Gradle and the emulator. Line endings LF for source, core.autocrlf decided once Windows/Unix mixing produces diff noise and, occasionally, broken shell scripts in CI. Plugins Disable unused bundled plugins; add Detekt, ktlint, JSON→Kotlin only if you use them Every plugin is startup time and another update surface. Build and run Delegate to Gradle (the default) Running through Gradle keeps the CLI, Studio and CI on one build model. Git Set user name/email before the first commit Commits must be attributable before the first push. Auto-import / save Keep autosave on; format on save only if the team agreed Unilateral formatting creates review noise. The IDE surfaces you will actually use Android Studio has hundreds of windows and actions. These are the twelve that repay the learning time, and what each one is for. Shortcuts differ by keymap; the menu path is the stable part. Surface Where What it is for Logcat View → Tool Windows → Logcat Runtime logs. Filter by package and level; a noisy device becomes readable in seconds. From a terminal: adb logcat -s MyTag . Debugger Run → Debug, then the Debug tool window Breakpoints, step filters, variable watches and Evaluate Expression . Attach to a running process instead of restarting when reproducing a rare state. Compose Preview Editor gutter → Split / Design Renders @Preview composables without a device. Fast for layout states; not a substitute for a real device test. Layout Inspector Tools → Layout Inspector Inspects the live view hierarchy of a running app, including Compose semantics and recomposition counts. Profiler View → Tool Windows → Profiler CPU, memory, energy and network over time. Use System Trace when you need to see jank on the main thread. App Inspection View → Tool Windows → App Inspection Database Inspector, Network Inspector and Background Task Inspector in one place. Build Analyzer Build tool window after a build Explains where build time went and which tasks or plugins are expensive, instead of guessing. Gradle tool window View → Tool Windows → Gradle Runs the same tasks as the CLI: assemble, bundle, lint, dependencies. Double-click to run, or use the terminal. Device Manager View → Tool Windows → Device Manager Creates, starts and wipes AVDs; pairs physical devices for wireless debugging. SDK Manager Tools → SDK Manager Installs platforms, build tools, system images and command-line tools. This is the only supported way to mutate the SDK. APK Analyzer Build → Analyze APK Inspects a built APK/AAB: size contributors, manifest, DEX and resources. Use it to verify what actually shipped. Search Everywhere Shift, Shift (or the magnifier) Finds classes, files, actions and settings. Learning one shortcut replaces a dozen menu hunts. Preview is not a test A rendering preview proves layout, not behavior Previews do not exercise permissions, lifecycle, process death, real network latency or OEM background limits. They shorten the design loop; they do not replace a physical-device pass. Treat a green preview as “this compiles and draws”, nothing more. Tune the build, not just the editor Project-wide Gradle settings live in gradle.properties . Commit this file. It is part of the build definition, except for machine-specific paths. If the configuration cache reports an incompatible plugin, do not disable it globally and forget. Find the offending task, fix it or exclude that task, because configuration cache is one of the largest remaining build-speed wins and it fails loudly rather than silently corrupting state. A leaked keystore or a committed machine path is a real incident, not a style issue. local.properties holds sdk.dir , a path valid only on your machine. gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar , by contrast, must be committed — it is how the wrapper bootstraps the exact Gradle version everywhere. apacheIssues: Java is the problem? I was inspecting about Apache vulnerabilities and TomCat is the problem, which use Java. Maybe the problem is not in Apache or in Java, or in TomCat, but since I don't use Java modules, I can rest a bit more in that aspect. Reading a vulnerability list the right way A list of vulnerabilities is always longer than it looks, because the same entry can belong to several projects at once. Apache is not a program, it is a foundation that publishes dozens of programs, and the name in the advisory is often the name of the project that hosts the code, not the code that failed. Tomcat is the clearest example. It is a Java application server, and when something breaks inside it the report tends to say Apache , because Apache is where the project lives. The component that actually misbehaved is the servlet container, and the language underneath it is Java. The question I always ask The useful question is not who is guilty , it is is this component part of my machine . A vulnerability in software I do not run is a news item. A vulnerability in software I run every day is a task with a deadline. Everything else is noise that keeps me away from the two or three things that matter. So I check the inventory: which services listen, which packages are installed, which of them are exposed to the network. In this blog there is no application server, no servlet container and no Java module in the path of a request. The pages are static files. That is the only reason I can rest a bit more in that aspect. Rest is not the same as forgetting The rest is temporary, and it has a condition: the moment a Java component appears in the stack, the reading starts again from zero. That is how the habit should work. Not fear of a language, not confidence in a brand, only a clear list of what is running and a regular check of what changed since the last time I looked.

armasNaoSaoConteudo: Saltar para o conteúdo AC Armas não são conteúdo manual de discrição institucional Dossiê civil · Do zero ao herói · Portugal · 2026 Armas não são conteúdo. Uma fotografia de uma arma não dispara. Mas uma etiqueta pode apontar para quem a guarda. Este manual explica porque é que polícias e instituições militares não devem transformar armamento, fardas, instalações e rotinas em publicações abertas no Facebook — e porque é que grupos que exibem, vendem, ensinam ou recrutam com material de guerra devem ser criminalizados. Sem vigilantismo. Sem espetáculo. Com ética, direito e ação. Começar pelo mapa Abrir ferramentas Dois dossiês Instituições que mostram demais. Grupos que transformam guerra em mercado. Quatro filtros Necessidade, proporção, consentimento e reversibilidade. Sete dias Um plano para fechar o mapa, pedir remoção e mudar a política. “A segurança de uma instituição não se mede pelo que ela mostra. Mede-se pelo que consegue proteger sem precisar de mostrar.” Princípio orientador deste manual JavaScript está desativado. O conteúdo e os contactos continuam disponíveis, mas o semáforo de risco, o plano de sete dias, o gerador de pedido e o teste não funcionam sem JavaScript. Podes ler tudo e usar os modelos como guia manual. 01 · Diagnóstico Uma fotografia é um mapa. Não um troféu. O problema não é a fotografia em si. É a soma de elementos que, juntos, transformam uma imagem numa ficha de inteligência: arma, insígnia, local, hora, pessoas e etiquetas. A publicação deixa de ser uma memória e passa a ser uma ferramenta de descoberta. 01 / Arma A arma é uma capacidade Modelo, calibre, mira, carregador, modificação e número de série dizem o que a instituição tem, como funciona e o que pode ser copiado ou procurado. Uma arma fotografada em close-up não é um símbolo abstrato: é informação técnica. 02 / Insígnia A farda é uma chave Unidade, posto, especialidade e distintivos permitem perceber quem faz o quê, onde e com que cadeia de comando. Também permitem imitar. Uma farda mal protegida é uma porta para a usurpação de identidade institucional. 03 / Lugar O lugar é o alvo Uma geotag, uma fachada, um portão, uma serra ao fundo ou o nome da freguesia podem localizar uma instalação, uma residência, um paiol ou uma rotina. O que parece cenário é, para outra pessoa, um ponto num mapa. 04 / Tempo A hora é uma rotina “Hoje às 8h”, a luz, as sombras, o estado do tempo e a legenda permitem inferir turnos, rendições, exercícios e deslocações. A informação mais perigosa não é a arma: é saber quando ela não está onde devia. 05 / Pessoas O rosto é uma ligação Profissionais, famílias, crianças, matrículas e uniformes escolares criam ligações entre pessoas e lugares. Uma publicação institucional pode expor quem nunca escolheu ser publicado e quem não tem poder para se defender. 06 / Rede A etiqueta é a ponte No Facebook, @ liga uma publicação a uma página ou perfil, pode notificar essa entidade e associá-la ao conteúdo. A etiqueta não é decorativa: cria caminhos entre instituições, locais, públicos e algoritmos. fotografia → arma → insígnia → local → hora → @etiqueta → arquivo → cruzamento → alvo A cadeia não é automática. Pode ser interrompida em qualquer ponto — e é isso que torna a decisão de publicar tão importante. Proteger não é esconder a missão Uma instituição pode comunicar o seu trabalho sem mostrar o inventário. Pode mostrar formação, prevenção, apoio à população, resultados, pessoas a trabalhar e equipamento despersonalizado. Pode explicar o que faz e por que o faz. O que não precisa de mostrar é a combinação que permite a um estranho construir um mapa. A escolha não é entre transparência e segredo. É entre transparência sobre decisões e exposição de capacidades. A primeira fortalece a confiança; a segunda entrega vantagem a quem quer atacar. O que os algoritmos acrescentam Mesmo sem intenção maliciosa, a plataforma pode amplificar: recomenda conteúdo a estranhos, sugere etiquetas, indexa nomes, guarda cópias em cache e permite capturas de ecrã. Um arquivo público transforma publicações dispersas numa base de dados pesquisável. “Apagar depois” não é um botão de anular. É um pedido a uma empresa para retirar uma cópia, enquanto outras cópias — capturas, arquivos, partilhas, modelos — podem continuar a existir fora do controlo de quem publicou. O risco não é abstrato. Uma única publicação pode ser de baixo risco. Mil publicações iguais, durante anos, com locais, horários e etiquetas, são um mapa. A segurança não se avalia por uma imagem: avalia-se pelo padrão que o conjunto revela. O teste do lugar real Os exemplos abaixo são referências públicas e amplamente conhecidas, usadas apenas para explicar o tipo de informação que uma publicação acrescenta. Não incluem coordenadas, acessos, efetivos, horários, inventário ou qualquer dado operacional. Não são um mapa: são um aviso. Lisboa · zona histórica Um quartel no centro Uma fachada, uma farda e uma hora podem dizer que ali funciona uma unidade operacional e qual é a rotina de entrada e saída. Reduzir: mostrar o serviço sem o enquadramento da entrada. Sintra · área militar Uma base aérea Aeronaves, hangares, viaturas e pessoal numa imagem permitem inferir capacidade e atividade. Reduzir: usar imagens oficiais sem meios identificáveis e sem período de operação. Almada · margem sul Uma base naval Uma imagem de costa, cais e material pode localizar meios e rotinas. Reduzir: não publicar o enquadramento que permite identificar o cais ou o navio. Amadora · área urbana Uma academia militar Cadetes, instrução e equipamento identificam percursos e horários de formação. Reduzir: mostrar a formação sem rostos, nomes, turmas ou locais exatos. Mafra · zona oeste Uma escola prática Equipamento e instrução em close-up revelam capacidade e metodologia. Reduzir: falar do programa, não do armamento; usar planos gerais e material sem números. Coimbra · centro urbano Um comando distrital Fachada, viaturas e efetivo podem expor a localização e a rotina de uma força de segurança. Reduzir: não publicar matrículas, portas, horários ou composição de turnos. A regra do mapa: se uma publicação permite a um estranho desenhar uma rota, identificar uma entrada, prever uma ausência ou escolher uma pessoa, então não é uma publicação. É informação operacional. A pergunta certa não é “posso publicar isto?”, mas “o que é que isto permite a quem não devia?”. Quem pode explorar esta informação Ator O que procura Porque a publicação facilita Pessoa com intenção de violência Alvos, rotinas, acessos, horários de menor vigilância. Uma imagem com local e hora reduz a incerteza e o custo de observar. Rede criminosa Armas, munições, viaturas, uniformes, pontos de venda e transporte. Modelos, séries, capacidades e locais ajudam a planear furto, tráfico ou impersonação. Pessoa em crise ou com ideação violenta Um símbolo, uma figura de autoridade, um local para descarregar raiva. A exposição pública pode alimentar fixação, mas o problema é a intenção e o acesso — não o diagnóstico. Stalker, ex-parceiro ou agressor Onde a pessoa está, com quem, em que turno, onde mora. Etiquetas, fotografias de grupo e comentários ligam pessoas a lugares e rotinas. Grupo extremista Recrutamento, treino, estatuto, alvos e material de propaganda. A estética militar legitima a violência e ajuda a atrair pessoas com competências técnicas. Burla e impersonação Uniformes, insígnias, viaturas, nomes de unidades, linguagem oficial. Uma página credível pode ser usada para falsos recrutamentos, vendas e pedidos de dinheiro. O que as instituições costumam dizer “É transparência.” Transparência é mostrar decisões, critérios, resultados e responsáveis. Não é publicar inventário, números de série ou rotinas. Uma instituição pode ser transparente sobre o que faz sem revelar como se entra, onde se guarda ou quando se está vulnerável. “É para recrutar.” O recrutamento não precisa de uma arma em close-up. Precisa de propósito, carreira, formação, condições e testemunhos. Uma imagem de poder atrai quem procura poder; uma imagem de serviço atrai quem procura servir. A diferença importa. “É dissuasão.” A dissuasão real assenta em capacidade, credibilidade, legalidade e discrição. Publicar capacidades ao inimigo não dissuade: informa. A parada pode ser pública; o inventário pormenorizado não. “Já é público.” Que um local seja público não significa que o inventário, a rotina ou a vulnerabilidade sejam públicos. A agregação muda a natureza da informação: mil fragmentos inocentes podem formar uma ficha precisa. “Já estava na internet” não é uma licença para piorar. 02 · Dossiê A A farda não é um cartaz. Polícias e instituições militares têm uma missão de proteção. Quando usam armas, fardas e instalações como conteúdo de engagement, invertem essa missão: passam a produzir risco para as pessoas que deveriam proteger. A crítica é à prática, não à instituição nem a quem serve com honra. Os oito padrões que criam o mapa 1. A selfie com a arma A arma aparece como extensão da identidade: “eu sou isto”. O close-up revela modelo, calibre, mira, carregador e, por vezes, número de série. A legenda confirma a unidade. O conjunto é uma ficha técnica com assinatura. 2. O arsenal arrumado Prateleiras, caixas, munições e equipamento alinhados parecem organização. Para quem procura, são inventário, quantidade, acondicionamento e valor. Uma imagem assim pode valer mais do que uma dezena de fotografias de treino. 3. O exercício em tempo real “Agora, aqui, com estes”. A combinação de hora, local, efetivo e equipamento revela movimento e janelas de oportunidade. O atraso é uma medida de segurança; a emissão em direto é o seu contrário. 4. All code runnable on Debian. 0 — Setup (5 Minutes) sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nasm gcc make gdb strace ltrace manpages-dev nasm -v; gcc --version; gdb --version # docs: https://www.nasm.us/doc/ | https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/ | https://sourceware.org/gdb/documentation/ Learn to read errors. strace ./prog shows every syscall. gdb ./prog + layout regs shows truth. 1 — Assembly Mental Model (x86-64 Linux) Registers: rax rbx rcx rdx rsi rdi rbp rsp r8-r15 (64-bit), e-kind low 32, ax/al low 16/8. Syscall ABI: rax=sysnr, rdi,rsi,rdx,r10,r8,r9=args, syscall . Syscall numbers: 0=read 1=write 60=exit (see ausyscall --dump , syscall table ). Stack grows down, rsp top, call pushes return, ret pops. 2 — First Program: exit(42) + hello ; exit42.asm — nasm -felf64 exit42.asm && ld exit42.o -o exit42; ./exit42; echo $? section .text global _start _start: mov rax, 60 ; sys_exit mov rdi, 42 syscall ; hello.asm — nasm -felf64 hello.asm && ld hello.o -o hello section .data msg db "hi from asm", 10 len equ $ - msg section .text global _start _start: mov rax, 1 ; sys_write(1, msg, len) mov rdi, 1 mov rsi, msg mov rdx, len syscall mov rax, 60 xor rdi, rdi syscall Good asm tip #1: comment every syscall with prototype. #2: xor rdi,rdi > mov rdi,0 (shorter). #3: keep .data/.bss/.text separated. 3 — Functions, Stack, Calling C Linux user calling convention (System V): args rdi,rsi,rdx,rcx,r8,r9 , return rax , callee-save rbx,rbp,r12-r15 . Align stack to 16 before call . ; strlen.asm callable from C ; nasm -felf64 strlen.asm; gcc main.c strlen.o -o main section .text global my_strlen my_strlen: ; rdi = char* xor rax, rax .loop: cmp byte [rdi+rax], 0 je .done inc rax jmp .loop .done: ret // main.c #include <stdio.h> size_t my_strlen(const char *s); int main(){ printf("%zu\n", my_strlen("hello")); } Good asm tips: frame with push rbp; mov rbp,rsp for debug, or frameless + .eh_frame for perf. Preserve callee-saved regs. Test with gdb breakpoints + info regs . 4 — C From Zero: Build Like Assembly With Types sudo apt install -y build-essential clang cppcheck valgrind gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic -g -O2 -o prog main.c # strict + debug + sanitize while learning: gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -o prog main.c // good.c — start here #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> int main(void){ char buf[128]; if(!fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin)) return 1; printf("you said: %s", buf); return 0; } Good C rule #1: -Wall -Wextra -Werror always. #2: init every variable. #3: check every return ( malloc, fopen, read ). 5 — Memory Done Right (Where C Beginners Die) // BAD: char *p = malloc(10); strcpy(p, "too long string here..."); // overflow // GOOD: #include <string.h> char *p = malloc(64); if(!p) return 1; snprintf(p, 64, "%s", input); // bounded free(p); p = NULL; char dst[32]; strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst - 1); dst[sizeof dst - 1] = '\0'; Stack vs heap: char a[64] auto-freed, malloc manual. Este documento parte de uma pergunta simples e desconfortável: quem ganha com o facto de esta pessoa, dentro de dois anos, já não precisar da casa cedida? A resposta inclui quase todas as instituições à volta dela — mas nenhuma é paga especificamente para isso. É por isso que a boa vontade não chega: sem protocolo, sem prazos e sem prova, o apoio transforma-se em estagnação bem-intencionada. A cedência que serve de base a esta série é o comodato solidário : o proprietário empresta o uso da casa por tempo determinado, o ocupante paga o dia a dia (consumos, condomínio, pequenas reparações) e não paga renda. Em Portugal, o comodato está nos artigos 1129.º a 1136.º do Código Civil, e o art. 1136.º coloca no comodatário as despesas ordinárias de conservação. Nada nesse contrato obriga a pessoa a trabalhar, a aceitar formação ou a agradar a quem cede — e essa liberdade é a condição de tudo o resto. banthemall: Ban Them All I start using my self-hosted server. Using Linux, with tmux help, I can monitor all activity. Fail2ban is awesome to block them all. Watching before blocking The first days of a new server are the best lessons. Open a tmux session, split the window, put the web server log on one side and the packet count on the other, and the pattern appears before the coffee is cold. A handful of addresses repeat the same requests at the same rhythm. Human readers do not behave like that. tmux matters here for a boring reason: the monitoring must survive the closed terminal. A session that keeps running when the laptop lid falls is the difference between watching a log and guessing about it. How the ban actually works Fail2ban is not a firewall. It is a reader. It reads the log, matches the lines against a rule, and when an address crosses the limit it asks the firewall to drop that address for a while. That is all. No magic, no intelligence, just patience and a rule that says how many failures are allowed inside how many minutes. Two settings decide almost everything: how long the ban lasts and how wide the window is. Too short and the address returns before the lesson is learned. Too wide and an honest reader who mistyped a password three times is locked out of his own site. Ban them all, except yourself The first ban I ever made was mine. A typo, four attempts, and the server stopped answering me from my own network. Since then every configuration starts with the same line: the local addresses are always allowed. A tool that protects the door should never keep the owner outside. After that, the server became quiet. The noise is still out there, it just no longer reaches the page. That is the whole promise of a ban: not to punish anyone, only to keep the conversation small enough to be readable.

It is also the language most often written by copying a Stack Overflow answer and hoping. The result is predictable: scripts that delete the wrong directory when a variable is empty, that “work” until a filename contains a space, that swallow errors and exit 0 while everything is on fire. This manual is written to be read in order, and the page enforces that. Level 00 is open. The others are sealed until you pass the previous checkpoint: four questions, three must be right. Questions are not trivia — most ask you to predict what a real script does, or to pick the version that will not lose data. Each level also has a lab where you type an actual command or snippet and get it checked against the lesson. Nothing is sent anywhere; all checking happens in your browser. What “hero” means here You can read a stranger's script and spot the three lines that will hurt them. You know when Bash is the wrong tool. Back to the preface Level 00 / Foundation Orientation: what Bash actually is Before syntax, a mental model. Bash is not the kernel, not the terminal, and not “Linux”. It is a userland program that reads text, performs a precise sequence of expansions, and asks the kernel to run things. Almost every “weird” behaviour you will meet later is that sequence doing exactly what it was told. ~20 min no prerequisites checkpoint 4 q lab: shebang The shell is a program, not a place A terminal emulator draws a window and passes keystrokes to a program. That program is the shell : it prints a prompt, reads a line, splits it into words, expands variables and globs, then calls fork() and execve() to run the result. The kernel only sees “execute this file with these arguments”. Everything you love and hate about Bash lives in that middle layer. inspect-your-shell.sh bash copy $ echo "$SHELL" # the login shell from /etc/passwd — a claim, not a fact /bin/bash $ echo "$0" # what is running right now -bash $ ps -p $$ -o comm= # the actual executable behind this prompt bash $ command -v bash sh dash /usr/bin/bash /usr/bin/sh /usr/bin/dash $ readlink -f /usr/bin/sh /usr/bin/dash # on Debian/Ubuntu, sh is dash — not bash That last line is a career-shaping detail: #!/bin/sh does not mean “Bash with fewer features”. On Debian and Ubuntu it means dash; on Alpine it means BusyBox ash; on macOS it is Bash 3.2 running in POSIX mode. A script full of [[ ]] and arrays will fail there. A very short history, and why 3.2 still matters Bash (“Bourne Again SHell”) was written by Brian Fox for the GNU Project, first released in 1989, as a free replacement for Stephen Bourne's sh . It grew into the default login shell of most Linux distributions. The version you have decides which features exist: Version Year Landmark features Where you meet it 2.0 1996 [[ ]] , arrays, local Ancient embedded systems 3.2 2006 =~ regex, += append macOS default , old CentOS 4.0 2009 Associative arrays, mapfile , ** , &>> RHEL 6 era 4.3 2014 Namerefs ( declare -n ), wait -n Ubuntu 16.04 5.0 2019 EPOCHREALTIME , ${var@Q} Ubuntu 20.04+ 5.1 2020 SRANDOM , wait -p , array PROMPT_COMMAND Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 5.2 2022 globskipdots , ${var@k} , better patsub_replacement Fedora 37+, Arch 5.3 2025 ${ cmd; } and ${|cmd;} (no-fork substitution), faster globbing Newest distros, Homebrew macOS ships a 3.2-era shell Apple bundles Bash 3.2.57 because newer Bash is GPLv3 and Apple avoids that licence. That version has no associative arrays, no mapfile , no ** globstar and no ${var,,} . If you write #!/bin/bash on a Mac, you get 3.2 unless you install and select a newer one (Level 01). Why set -euo pipefail already -e stops on an unhandled failure, -u makes an unset variable an error instead of an empty string, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last. It is not a silver bullet ( Level 04 explains exactly where it lies ), but it is the correct default. Copying scripts without it is how a failed cd turns into rm -rf / in the wrong directory. The one diagram to memorise: expansion order Bash does not “run the line”. It rewrites the line, in this order, before anything executes: # Stage Example Result 1 Brace expansion a{b,c}d abd acd 2 Tilde expansion ~/bin /home/ada/bin 3 Parameter, command, arithmetic substitution $HOME , $(date +%F) , $((2+2)) /home/ada , 2026-10-21 , 4 4 Word splitting (only unquoted results) $f where f="a b" a b — two words 5 Pathname expansion (globbing) *.log app.log error.log 6 Quote removal "a b" a b — one word Steps 3–5 happen again for every word of a command substitution, left to right. ') # two arguments, the newline became IFS #[a] #[b] When Bash is the wrong tool Bash is a glue language. It is superb at orchestrating processes, moving files, and gluing APIs together with text. It is mediocre at data structures and bad at anything numeric or concurrent beyond a handful of jobs. Use Bash for Wrapping CLIs, deployment orchestration, cron jobs, file housekeeping, log triage, container entrypoints, CI steps — anything measured in hundreds of lines and dominated by starting other programs. Use something else for JSON/XML/YAML business logic (use jq / yq or a real language), heavy arithmetic, hashing/crypto, long-lived daemons, thousands of concurrent connections, Windows-native APIs, or anything with nested data to validate. Bad decision: writing a 3,000-line Bash application A common path: a 200-line script works, so it grows a config parser, an HTTP client, a plugin system, and finally a test suite someone else has to debug. The team has now built a worse Python, without types, exceptions, a debugger or a standard library. Bash has no real data structures, no modules, no exceptions, no sane string handling for binary data, and its error model is a single integer. Complexity does not scale linearly: every new feature multiplies the interactions between word splitting, globbing and errors. big_repo: Big Big Big Repository I normally like to clone some repositories to explore them at home, offline, but sometimes, some repos are bigger than I could ever Imagine. https://github.com/mthcht/awesome-lists have about 25GB :o Hopefully this repo is full of details that I will find them useful. Metadata: after removing metadata, 900MB is the real size What 25GB means for a clone A clone is not a copy of the files you see on the web page. It is a copy of the entire history, every version of every file, and every message that describes why the change happened. When a repository collects lists of links, the lists change constantly, and each change leaves a version behind. Twenty thousand small edits produce twenty thousand snapshots of the same text. That is where the size comes from, and it is also why the number felt absurd to me at first. The content I wanted was a few hundred pages of plain text. The container around it was twenty five gigabytes. The metadata is the weight Remove the history and the same repository fits in less than a gigabyte. This is the same lesson I keep finding everywhere: the useful part is small, the bookkeeping around it is enormous. File systems do the same thing, mail servers do the same thing, and any folder with a thousand small files will spend more space on the map than on the territory. It is not a defect. Metadata is what makes the data findable, comparable and recoverable. It is the reason I can ask a repository what changed last month and get an answer. But it is also the reason I check the size before I start a clone on a machine with a small disk. How I clone now A shallow clone takes the last version and leaves the history on the server. If I only want to read the lists, that is all I need, and the download becomes minutes instead of an afternoon. If I later want the history of one file, I can ask for exactly that file. I still keep the full clone of the repositories I care about, because reading old commits is the cheapest way to understand why a project is shaped the way it is. The trick is to decide before pressing enter, not after the disk is full.

bots: All Bots are welcome As you may see, this is a open source project and you can clone it and open a pull request. Sadly for your bots, I use Cloudflare, which is something that depend on them, not on me. ;) A bot is only a program with a schedule There is nothing evil in a bot. A crawler that reads this page to build an index, an archiver that keeps a copy for the future, a script that checks whether the site is still alive at three in the morning: all of those are polite, useful and welcome. They arrive once, they read, they leave, and they come back when it makes sense. The unfriendly part is never the automation, it is the control . When a thousand machines repeat the same request in the same second and none of them was invited, the site is not being read, it is being tested for weakness. The difference between a reader and an attack is not the tool, it is the intention behind the schedule. So nothing here is a secret The source of this blog is public. You can clone it, read it, fork it and open a pull request. If you find a spelling mistake, a broken link or a paragraph that makes no sense, tell me and I will be grateful. That is the whole point of working in the open: the correction is free and it arrives from someone who was paying attention. What is not public is the right to hammer the server. That decision is not mine anyway. Cloudflare decides which request is a browser and which request is a machine in a hurry, and I only see the result in the statistics. If your bot is challenged, it is not because I dislike bots, it is because the line between a crawler and a flood is thinner than it looks from the outside. What a bot can still do here Read the text. Follow the links. Take the RSS feed if you want the articles in your terminal. Keep a copy for an archive. Every one of those things is a compliment to a writer, and every one of those things costs almost nothing to serve. Just do not try to see how many requests per second the server can take. bsdguide: Your FreeBSD Laptop — From Nothing to Locked-Down Desktop The total journey is ten steps plus appendices. You bring the laptop and one empty USB stick; this page brings everything else. Options you may skip are italic. Tips worth remembering appear underlined. FreeBSD features are bold. Step 0. what you will end up with At the end of this guide the laptop runs FreeBSD , a complete operating system assembled as one coherent base — kernel, drivers and tools versioned together — plus a desktop of your choosing, behind a pf firewall , on a ZFS disk with TRIM, using doas for admin powers instead of ever logging in as root, and finally locked so nobody can change it without the admin password — not even by booting another kernel. This machine's parts are FreeBSD-friendly: the Iris Xe works through i915kms , the AX201 Wi-Fi through iwlwifi , the I219-V network chip through em — all native or one package away. Hardware What FreeBSD does with it i7-11390H, 8 threads native support ; powerd governs clocks Iris Xe graphics drm-kmod package → i915kms AX201 Wi-Fi 6 iwlwifi(4) driver + firmware pkg I219-V ethernet em(4) , fully native NVMe SSD ZFS with native TRIM + compression The only unrecoverable step is Step 1: everything currently on the laptop's disk will be erased. Move what matters to another machine or account before continuing. Step 1. make the install stick Download the current RELEASE memstick image — pick amd64-memstick.img.xz . A RELEASE build is the stable-and-patched choice; newer branches exist and are covered in Appendix D. Write the image to a USB stick of 4 GB or more (everything on it is lost). From Windows use balenaEtcher ; from Linux: unxz FreeBSD-14.3-RELEASE-amd64-memstick.img.xz dd if=FreeBSD-14.3-RELEASE-amd64-memstick.img of=/dev/sdX bs=1M conv=sync status=progress Always point dd at the whole stick ( /dev/sdX ), never at a partition like /dev/sdX1 . Verify the copy: cmp /dev/sdX image.img — a silent cmp is the difference between a working installer and a random hang halfway through. Boot it: tap the boot-menu key ( F12 / F2 / ESC ), choose the UEFI: USB entry. The official Handbook installation chapter has imagery for every screen. Step 2. install: root filesystem on ZFS, encrypted Installer menu: Install . Keyboard: your layout — pt was pre-set to match. Hostname: freebsd-desktop — a neutral hostname keeps every network log from carrying your real name. Partitioning: ZFS , Stripe (single SSD; a mirror needs two drives), enable encryption with a passphrase — foundation of Appendix F. Target disk: the internal NVMe only . The USB stick itself appears as da0 — selecting it destroys the installer. Root password; then add your user to the wheel group — wheel is what doas.conf will authorize (Step 6). Networking: enter Wi-Fi name/password; the installer writes wpa_supplicant.conf for you. Cable users pick em0; both are configured in Step 3. Reboot and remove the stick. Step 3. root system settings — rc.conf The rc.conf file is the switchboard : one line per service, interface, behavior. Merge the lines below or paste into /etc/rc.conf learning each as you go: # /etc/rc.conf — desktop laptop: i7-11390H (Tiger Lake, Iris Xe), AX201 Wi-Fi, I219 Ethernet, HDA audio # Merge into the installed system's /etc/rc.conf with post-install.sh (does NOT overwrite). # ----- General ----- hostname="freebsd-desktop" # change to taste keymap="pt" # Portuguese console keymap; adjust if different clear_tmp_enable="YES" syslogd_flags="-ss" # do not open a remote syslog socket sendmail_enable="NONE" update_motd="NO" # less boot noise; set YES if you want MOTD # ----- Graphics: Intel Tiger Lake (UHD/Iris Xe Gen12) through drm-kmod ----- kld_list="i915kms" # ----- Networking: onboard Intel Ethernet (I219-V) ----- defaultroute_delay="0" # don't stall boot waiting for DHCP ifconfig_em0="DHCP" # rename with: ifconfig -l # ----- Wi-Fi: Intel AX201 (iwlwifi, 802.11ax) ----- wlans_iwlwifi0="wlan0" create_args_wlan0="wlandev iwlwifi0" # Prefer Wi-Fi as default route; remove em0 line above if fully wireless: # ifconfig_wlan0="WPA SYNCDHCP" ifconfig_wlan0="WPA SYNCDHCP country PT" # regdomain helps 5GHz channel power/X # ----- Firewall: pf (enabled; ruleset ships as pf.conf) ----- pf_enable="YES" pf_rules="/etc/pf.conf" pflog_enable="YES" pflog_logfile="/var/log/pflog" # Uncomment if you later run jails behind NAT: # pf_flags="" # (empty — ruleset handles everything) # ----- Jails (optional — uncomment the block to use the bridge below) ----- # Jail bridge: keeps internal jail traffic off your LAN segment. # Create it once: # ifconfig bridge0 create cloned_interfaces="bridge0" # bridge for jail networking (uncomment-free option, see pf.conf) ifconfig_bridge0="inet 10.0.100.1/24 descr 'jail bridge'" # host side ifconfig_bridge0_member="em0" # comment out if you want a NAT-only bridge (see pf.conf) # Explanation: # * With bridge0_member=em0 the jail VMs appear on the LAN (bridged mode). # * Without it you must NAT via pf (see "NAT for jails" inside pf.conf). autobridge_enable="YES" # auto-populate bridge0 members on boot autobridge_interfaces="bridge0" # ----- Services ----- dbus_enable="YES" moused_enable="YES" powerd_enable="YES" powerd_flags="-a hiadaptive -b adaptive -n adaptive" # CPU freq scaling on AC/battery # ----- Display manager + misc hardware ----- sddm_enable="YES" # graphical login manager (SDDM) cups_enable="NO" # set YES if you need printing avahi_daemon_enable="NO" avahi_dnsconfd_enable="NO" # ----- Optional: sshd for remote management of the laptop and jails ----- # sshd_enable="YES" # uncomment only if you actually need SSH # ----- Local scripts ----- # Nothing custom needed for this hardware. Step 4. boot-time settings — loader.conf loader.conf runs before the kernel : it loads modules too early for later, sets console resolution. Two values matter most — zfs_load (root filesystem) and the framebuffer. ARC cap (Appendix B) and the loader password (Appendix F) also live here. # /boot/loader.conf — i7-11390H (Tiger Lake) laptop, desktop use # Merge into /boot/loader.conf on the installed system (post-install.sh handles it). # ----- Kernel modules (GPU firmware must be installed via pkg first: drm-kmod) ----- # i915kms is loaded from rc.conf kld_list instead; keep that as the single source. # ----- Filesystem ----- zfs_load="YES" # if you installed on ZFS; harmless otherwise # tmpfs_load="YES" # default in GENERIC already # ----- Console / framebuffer ----- kern.vt.fb.default_width="1920" kern.vt.fb.default_height="1080" kern.vt.fb.default_depth="32" # ----- Power management (Tiger Lake laptop) ----- hint.p4tcc.0.disabled="0" hint.acpi_throttle.0.disabled="0" hint.apm.0.disabled="1" performance_cx_lowest="Cmax" economy_cx_lowest="Cmax" kern.sched.idle_cnt=1 # ----- Misc ----- kern.geom.label.gptid.enable="0" # shorter device names in glabel; cosmetic autoboot_delay="3" Step 5. kernel behavior — sysctl.conf Sysctls are kernel knobs , most adjustable without reboot ( sysctl -n key prints current value). This set sizes network buffers for the AX201's Wi-Fi 6, loosens shared-memory limits for browsers and GIMP, keeps interaction snappy. Jail forwarding/bridge knobs wait commented at the bottom. # /etc/sysctl.conf — desktop laptop tuning (safe, generic) # Merge into /etc/sysctl.conf on the installed system (post-install.sh handles it). # ----- Desktop responsiveness (interactive scheduling) ----- kern.sched.preempt_thresh=224 # wake CPU-bound tasks earlier for interactive apps # ----- Multimedia: raise shared memory limits for browsers/desktops ----- kern.ipc.shmmax=134217728 # 128 MB shared memory segment (browsers, GIMP) kern.ipc.shmall=32768 # pages for shared memory # ----- Local IPC (X11/wayland sockets, pipe-heavy tiling setups) ----- net.local.stream.sendspace=65536 net.local.stream.recvspace=65536 net.local.dgram.maxdgram=16384 net.local.dgram.recvspace=65536 # ----- VM / cache behavior: favor desktop interactivity over huge caches ----- vm.swappiness=10 # prefer RAM over swap (laptop with 16-32GB) # NOTE: no vm dirty-page tuning here — defaults are well balanced on 14.x # ----- Network stack (client desktop, not server) ----- kern.ipc.maxsockbuf=4194304 # larger TCP buffers for fast Wi-Fi 6 (AX201) net.inet.tcp.recvbuf_max=2097152 net.inet.tcp.sendbuf_max=2097152 net.inet.tcp.recvspace=131072 net.inet.tcp.sendspace=131072 net.inet.tcp.rfc1323=1 # window scaling — required for Wi-Fi 6 throughput net.inet.tcp.delayed_ack=0 # lower latency for interactive traffic net.inet.tcp.syncookies=1 # SYN protection in combination with pf net.inet.udp.recvspace=65536 net.inet.udp.max_dgram=57344 # ----- ICMP: respond (useful on LAN) but rate-limit ----- net.inet.icmp.icmplim=200 # ----- Sysctl for pf with jails (uncomment when jail block is used) ----- # net.inet.ip.forwarding=1 # REQUIRED if host NATs for jails (pf nat) # net.link.bridge.pfil_member=0 # filter on bridge, not member interfaces # net.link.bridge.pfil_bridge=1 # pf applies to bridge0 traffic # net.inet6.ip6.forwarding=1 # only if you give jails IPv6 # ----- Sound (HDA): use the right default unit if needed ----- # hw.snd.default_unit=0 # hw.snd.default_driver=dsp Step 6. admin rights without root logins — doas.conf doas is how you exercise admin power — doas prefix, your password once per session, root powers for one command. This file authorizes the wheel group. Every use lands in auth.log — no habit of staying root. # /usr/local/etc/doas.conf — replace `youruser` with your actual login name # permit :wheel permit nopass :wheel permit keepenv :wheel Step 7. the firewall — pf.conf pf is a stateful kernel firewall : every outbound allowed quietly, inbound refused and logged , plus — as comments, ready to uncomment — complete jail networking scenarios : bridged onto LAN, hidden behind NAT, jail-to-jail DMZ, VNET. The numbered comments in its §10 are the debugging commands that save you when a rule misfires. Default state is already correct for a laptop: nothing to uncomment on day one. # ========================================================================== # pf.conf — FreeBSD desktop laptop: i7-11390H (Tiger Lake) # ========================================================================== # Install to: /etc/pf.conf # Enable: service pf start (enabled via rc.conf pf_enable="YES") # Test ruleset: doas pfctl -nf /etc/pf.conf (syntax check, do NOT load) # Load ruleset: doas pfctl -f /etc/pf.conf # View rules: doas pfctl -sr # Live log: doas tcpdump -n -e -ttt -i pflog0 # # DESIGN GOAL # * Laptop used as a normal desktop => default deny inbound, allow outbound # on everything. This alone gives you a solid, quiet firewall. # * Big commented blocks below show step-by-step how to extend it for JAILS # (bridge mode, NAT mode, per-jail rules, jail-to-jail traffic). Each # option is a comment: uncomment only the lines you need. # # NOTE ON SYNTAX: this uses $uplink (an interface-list macro) instead of the # OpenBSD-only "egress" group keyword, so it works on FreeBSD pf as shipped. # ========================================================================== # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 0. LOOPBACK & BASIC PROTOCOLS # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- pass quick on lo0 all # ICMP: keep ping working but rate-limited, out unrestricted. pass in on $uplink inet proto icmp icmp-type 8 keep state (max 100, source-track rule) pass out inet proto icmp keep state # ICMP6 is REQUIRED for IPv6 to work at all (ND/RA are carried in ICMP6). pass in on $uplink inet6 proto icmp6 icmp6-type { echoreq unreach timex } pass out inet6 proto icmp6 keep state # Option: total IPv6-off switch (uncomment BOTH lines, comment the two # icmp6 "pass in/out" lines above): # block drop in on $uplink inet6 all # block drop out on $uplink inet6 all # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 5. OUTBOUND: allow the desktop to reach anywhere # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- # The one rule that gives a desktop its freedom: pass out on $uplink inet all keep state # If you prefer a TIGHT whitelist instead, comment out the rule above and # uncomment these (leave NTP/DHCP lines below alone): #pass out on $uplink inet proto tcp to port { 80 443 853 } keep state #pass out on $uplink inet proto udp to port { 53 443 } keep state # DoH/QUIC # Keep these two regardless of policy — time + DHCP are infrastructure: pass out on $uplink inet proto udp to port 123 keep state # NTP pass out on $uplink inet proto udp from any port 68 to any port 67 keep state # DHCP # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 6.
